question: What is a modern data warehouse (RDW plus data lake), how does data flow through it, and when is it appropriate?
contributions: Describes the five-stage MDW data journey
Lists pros and cons of MDW
Fictitious case study of an SMP-based MDW

limits: No measurements: pros/cons, the 10 TB threshold and the case study (fictitious, 'a fictitious midsized pharmaceutical company') are author judgement.
The PDF has no title page, no author name, no book title; attribution to Serra rests on external information, only consistent with first-person voice and 'Chapter N' cross-references.
Product names (Synapse, Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake) reflect 2024 market.
practices: If data is small (say under 10 TB), an MDW is still a good choice (p. 137).
Very small, certain-not-to-grow data may justify an SMP RDW instead of MPP (p. 137, p. 147).
Bypassing the lake for relational reference tables is acceptable but loses backup and single-source-of-truth (p. 140).
Choose among stepping stones by needs, infrastructure, budget (p. 143).
To make all-in-one a stepping stone to an MDW, add an RDW (p. 147).

terms.definition: combines an RDW with a data lake; at least some data must be replicated to an RDW
cloud data lake added next to a large on-prem EDW to hold big data; primary data remains in the EDW
lake used solely as temporary staging and refining area, not for querying or reporting
all reporting and querying done on the data lake, no RDW
a dedicated space to do data experimentation, exploration, and preliminary analysis without affecting the other layers
an advanced layer built onto the MDW to enhance data accessibility, security, discoverability, and availability
